analysis.one_liner: Removes the cap on what nonparticipating doctors may bill Medicare patients and voids state balance-billing protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote and died in committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare, doctors who do not formally participate in the program can charge patients some amount above what Medicare pays, but federal law caps that extra charge. This bill would erase that cap entirely and also forbid any state from limiting how much a physician may bill a patient over what an insurer or health plan recognizes as the payment amount. In practice, patients would owe whatever a doctor chooses to charge on top of insurance or Medicare payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who decline to participate in Medicare and insurers' networks: they could bill patients unlimited amounts above the recognized payment rate, with no federal or state ceiling.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Medicare 'limiting charge' rules that cap how much a nonparticipating physician may charge a beneficiary above the Medicare-approved amount [S2] [S3].
Prohibits states from imposing any limit on the charges a physician may impose relative to recognized payment amounts under any health plan, and voids existing state limits [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and privately insured patients, who would owe unlimited extra charges whenever they see a doctor outside the program or network.

drawbacks.text: Patients, including seniors on fixed incomes, could face unlimited surprise charges from any doctor who does not take Medicare assignment, with no state law able to protect them [S2] [S3].
Because the preemption covers limits 'under any health plan or otherwise,' it would override state balance-billing protections for privately insured patients as well, not just Medicare [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows to physicians, who gain the right to charge patients unlimited amounts above the recognized payment rate. The cost falls directly on patients, especially seniors, who lose both the federal cap and any state protection against balance billing. The bill offers patients no offsetting benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Feeney introduced the bill on December 17, 2007, with 17 Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, which sent it to their health subcommittees, where no action followed [S5].
The bill saw no further action and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and state regulators are better off, since the federal charge cap and state balance-billing protections remain in force. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and state protections stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Tom Feeney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Medicare limiting charges and preempt state balance-billing limits.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors were Republicans and no chamber ever voted on the bill, so no recorded opposition or vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would let doctors who do not accept Medicare assignment bill patients unlimited amounts above the Medicare-approved rate, and void every state limit on charges. The gain comes directly out of patients' pockets.
Federal preemption would strip states of the power to cap balance billing, leaving their consumer-protection laws void.
In-network contracts would still cap what members owe, but unlimited out-of-network charges could shift costs to patients and complicate plan design.
